paragraphs.text:
Let a radius vector rotate uniformly with angular speed $\omega_0$, and represent it by $\overrightarrow{OA}$.
We examine only its projection on the $O_1X$ axis: the corresponding position on that axis (Figure $9$).
At the starting instant ($t=0$), let the radius point in the positive direction of the $O_1X$ axis.

This initial alignment fixes the starting phase.
At that instant, the projection of $\overrightarrow{OA}$ is longest and equals the radius length:
$|\overrightarrow{OA}|=x_{\mathrm{m}}$.

That length is also the amplitude of the projection's back-and-forth motion.
The projection has a sign, showing which side of its equilibrium position it lies on.

As the radius vector $\overrightarrow{OA}$ rotates uniformly, denote its angle from the $O_1X$ axis by $\varphi$.
Starting from the alignment just chosen, the accumulated rotation angle is proportional to elapsed time:
$\varphi=\omega_0t$.

The angle here tracks the rotation continuously.
It is not limited to the smaller angle between two lines.

On the $O_1X$ axis, denote the radius vector's signed projection by $x$.
Its length and direction depend on the rotation angle and can be described using cosine:
$x=x_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\varphi=x_{\mathrm{m}}\cos\omega_0t$.
Replacing the angle by its time-dependent expression tells us how the projection changes with time.

This projection changes back and forth according to a cosine law, so its motion is simple harmonic.
The statement concerns the projection on the axis.

The ball itself continues around the circle;
it does not move back and forth along that axis.

We can make this projection visible as a shadow.
Fix a ball to a disk that rotates uniformly, and shine parallel light toward it in a direction parallel to the disk's plane.
Place a screen perpendicular to the light's direction to receive the ball's shadow (Figure $10$).

Take the projected position of the disk's center, $O_1$, as the origin for the shadow's displacement.
The shadow's upward and downward displacement then equals the projection of the radius vector $\overrightarrow{OA}$ on a vertical axis.
Because that projection varies harmonically, the shadow moves up and down harmonically.

The ball moves around a circle.
We observe its projection, not a new straight-line motion of the ball itself.

Hang a weight from a spring where the same parallel light can reach it.
First place the weight at equilibrium and adjust its suspension so that its shadow is at the same height as the disk center's shadow.
We can then compare their upward and downward displacements from their respective equilibrium positions.

Move the weight upward from equilibrium by a distance $x_{\mathrm{m}}$, then release it without an extra push.
Choose that distance to equal the radius of the ball's circular path, so the two shadows can have equal amplitudes.
Choose the disk's rotation rate to match the weight's oscillation frequency, and start both motions together at their uppermost positions (Figure $11$).

Under these conditions, the two shadows can move together with matching positions and directions.
Treat the spring's restoring force as linear and resistance as negligible during the observation.
**The spring weight and the shadow of the uniformly rotating ball follow the same displacement law.**

The disk does not drive the spring.
This experiment compares their displacement laws.
The known harmonic motion of the ball's shadow illustrates the spring weight's harmonic motion.
